title: Benghal Dayflower: How to Spot and Control It in Rainfed Rice
metaTitle: Benghal Dayflower in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Benghal dayflower, or alikbangon, roots again from broken stems. Learn to spot its blue flowers in rainfed rice and how to remove it for good.
excerpt: Benghal dayflower is a fleshy, creeping weed with small blue flowers that grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It spreads by seed and by broken stem pieces, so careless weeding can make it worse. This page shows how to spot it early and how to control it for good.

heroImage.alt: Benghal dayflower (Commelina benghalensis), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This weed belongs to the dayflower family. Farmers call it alikbangon, gatilang or kulasi. Benghal dayflower grows in rainfed lowland rice fields, mainly on soil that stays moist but has no standing water. Each flower opens for only a day, and that habit gives the dayflower its name.

Most plants live as annuals, though some carry on as perennials. It also spreads in two ways. It sets seed, and its fleshy stems take root again when broken pieces lie on moist soil. This plant can even form small flowers and seeds below the ground, on short underground stems. That is why it can return after hand weeding that looked thorough.

Look low. The stems feel fleshy and juicy, and they creep along the ground before they turn upward. The leaves grow one at a time along the stem, widest in the middle and shaped like a broad oval. It sits in the broadleaf group because its leaves look wide and flat, but its veins run side by side, unlike most broadleaves. The blue flowers have three or four petals, two or three large and one small.

items: Fleshy, juicy stems creeping along the ground before they bend upward.
Broad oval leaves, widest in the middle, growing one at a time along the stem.
Small blue flowers with two or three large petals and one small one.
Leaf veins running side by side, even though the leaves look wide like a broadleaf.
New shoots rising from stem pieces left behind after weeding.

blocks.text:
Benghal dayflower spreads low and wide, so it covers the soil between rice hills and takes the water and fertilizer your palay needs. Its creeping stems crowd young rice, and the fleshy mats keep the ground shaded and damp. Insects, rats and other pests find shelter under them.

The bigger cost lies in how hard it is to clear. Pulled stems that stay on the field can root again. Some plants also live on past one season. So a field with dayflower may need several rounds of weeding, which adds to your labor cost every crop. Its seeds can also mix with harvested grain.

items: Never leave pulled stems lying on moist soil. Collect every piece in a sack and carry it out, since fleshy fragments root again.
Dig out the base of the plant with a small tool instead of just pulling the top, because it can form seeds on short underground stems.
Dry the pulled plants fully on a tarp or hard ground away from the field before you compost them.
Check the field again one to two weeks after weeding and remove any new shoots while they are small.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Benghal dayflower down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Benghal Dayflower Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Benghal Dayflower?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Benghal Dayflower

items.q: What is Benghal dayflower called in Tagalog?
items.a: Farmers call it alikbangon, gatilang or kulasi, depending on the region. A close relative, the climbing dayflower, shares the names alikbangon and gatilang. To tell them apart, compare the leaves. This species has broad oval leaves, widest in the middle, while the climbing kind has narrower, lance shaped leaves.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with prevention: plant clean seed and keep the field level so water covers the soil. Hand weed early, dig out the base, and remove every piece of stem from the field, because fragments root again. If you use a herbicide, pick one made for broadleaf weeds that suits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does dayflower keep coming back after weeding?
items.a: It has three ways to survive. Broken pieces of its fleshy stem take root again on moist soil. It also makes seeds, including some from small flowers that form below the ground. Besides that, some plants live as perennials. So pull carefully, remove every fragment, and check the field again after a week or two.
